title: Story Bias
hook: A clean plot can make missing evidence feel like a finished case.
coreIdea: Story bias makes coherent narratives feel truer than incomplete evidence, especially when sequence gets mistaken for causality.
counterintuition: A good story can help you remember facts, but it can also smuggle in causes that were never tested. The safer move is to mark the plot, then ask which links are evidence and which links are glue.
tryThisNow: Take one neat explanation you believe and draw its three causal links. Put a question mark on any link without evidence.
keyTakeaway: Use stories to organize evidence, not to replace the missing parts of it.

breakdown.fastRead:
An open-loop list sits beside the referee ratings after a controversial final. Simon hears the same plot everywhere: the referee lost control early, so the match turned rough, so the score became unfair. The story is smooth. The evidence is not.

Story bias appears when a coherent plot feels more convincing than the raw facts deserve. Events that happened in sequence get tied together as cause and effect. Missing pieces are filled in because the mind dislikes loose ends.

A neat arc is not a proof chain.

The correction is to mark each causal link, ask what evidence supports it, and leave blanks where the story is only joining dots.
breakdown.deepRead:
The open-loop list in Simon's federation file has five unresolved questions: two missed calls, one injured player, a weather delay, a coach's complaint, and a late penalty. The match narrative makes them feel connected. The referee looked nervous, then play got rough, then the losing team blamed the official. Simon writes story bias on the list and separates sequence from cause.

Stories are useful because they compress the world. They help memory, explain motives, and make a pile of facts easier to carry. The danger starts when the compression hides uncertainty. A story can turn after into because. It can turn one angry witness into the voice of the whole crowd. It can turn a messy set of causes into a single villain, hero, or lesson.

Plot is where uncertainty often goes to disappear.

A better review asks link by link. Did the early missed call change player behavior, or did the match already have a high foul rate? Did rough play cause the late penalty, or did fatigue and rain matter more? Did the final score become unfair, or did both teams adjust badly? The story may survive those questions. If it does, it will be stronger. If it does not, the rating should not punish a referee for a plot the evidence cannot hold.

An oncology dropout table makes the stakes more serious. Ruth sees a news alert queue about one patient who left a trial after side effects, and a reporter wants a clear story: the treatment drove patients away. Ruth writes causality on the queue and asks for all dropout reasons before changing the patient-information sheet.

A story that explains everything may have skipped the hard part.
breakdown.fullRead:
A clipboard snaps shut in the immigration appeal office while Eva reads a file with three dates highlighted. The applicant lost a job, missed a filing deadline, and received a removal notice. The appeal volunteer has a ready plot: job loss caused the missed filing, which caused the notice. Eva circles plot on the clipboard and asks what each link actually shows.

This bias has its grip because humans do not like fragments. A fragment asks us to hold tension. A story releases it. Once the story arrives, recall improves, confidence rises, and gaps feel smaller than they are. That is helpful when the story is built from evidence. It is dangerous when the story supplies the evidence.

E. M. Forster drew the classic line with kings and queens: one version gives sequence, another adds grief and turns sequence into plot. The difference is causality. That small literary distinction matters in decisions because adding a cause changes what you do next.

Which sentence did you add that was not in the file?

Eva uses that question on the appeal. The job loss is documented. The missed filing is documented. The emotional state between them is not. The volunteer may be right, but the office cannot treat the missing link as fact. Eva requests pay records, email logs, and clinic notes before ranking the appeal's urgency. The story becomes a hypothesis, not the verdict.

A climate fund pitch carries the same risk in a more polished form. You are holding a sealed envelope with a founder's impact story inside. The pitch says a flood destroyed a village, the founder built a tool, and donations will prevent the next disaster. Leo, the fund analyst, marks Forster risk on the envelope before the investment meeting. He must decide whether the plot proves impact or whether adoption rates, maintenance records, and local partners need to carry that claim.

This pause can feel like cruelty because stories often contain real pain. A painful story deserves respect. It does not deserve exemption from evidence. If a story is true, the missing links can be checked. If the links cannot be checked, the decision should say so plainly instead of letting the plot finish the work.

Story bias is also a recall machine. The version with motive and consequence is easier to remember than the version with loose facts. That ease of recall then feeds confidence. A call-center complaint script can become the official explanation for churn because everyone remembers the one customer who shouted, left, and posted online. The quiet billing failures vanish because they never became a story.

So keep stories, but audit them. Underline every because, therefore, led to, proved, and revealed. Ask which words are supported by records and which words are narrative glue. Then decide from the supported links, not from the satisfaction of a clean ending.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Story bias turns coherence into confidence. Readers need a way to keep narrative useful while refusing to let it invent causality.

examples.scenario: The federation review room is still smelling of turf tape at 8:30 a.m. when Simon opens the referee file and finds an open-loop list beside the match video. Everyone repeats the same plot about lost control. Before rating the referee, Simon must decide whether the story links are proven, so he writes story bias on the list.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the timeline from the causal claims. Score only the calls and control choices the video supports.
examples.whyItMatters: The match may have a story, but the rating needs evidence for each link. A clean plot should not become a career penalty.

Ruth must choose: rewrite the patient sheet from the vivid story or count every dropout reason first, so she writes causality on the alert queue.
examples.whatToDo: Complete the dropout table before changing the explanation. Let the patient story prompt a check, not become the causal answer.
examples.whyItMatters: The story may contain a real warning, but causality needs the full dropout pattern. One narrative cannot carry the whole trial.

examples.scenario: Paper edges rasp under Eva's thumb in the appeal office as she clips three dated forms to a clipboard. "The job loss caused the missed filing," a volunteer says. Eva marks plot and weighs whether to accept the neat chain or request the records that show how the dates connect. Before the room moves on, Paper must decide whether to accept the story or run the marked check.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the sequence, but leave the causal link open until records support it. Rank urgency from documented facts and stated uncertainty.
examples.whyItMatters: The plot may be true, but the missing link changes the appeal. A neat chain should not outrun the file.

examples.scenario: Which influencer campaign worked, the comeback story or the discount code? Henrik answers after the season by spreading an invoice stack beside the sales report. The athlete's injury comeback had become the campaign legend. Henrik marks story risk and reshapes the review so it will compare code use, margin, and repeat buyers.
examples.whatToDo: Respect the story, then test whether it produced profitable buyers. Renew based on sales evidence, not the emotional arc alone.
examples.whyItMatters: A good story can make a campaign feel successful before the numbers agree. The postmortem keeps emotion from replacing the invoice stack.

reviewCards.front: A sequence of events makes a clear story. What should you check?
reviewCards.back: Check which causal links are supported by evidence and which links were added to make the story feel complete.

reviewCards.front: Why does story bias feel convincing?
reviewCards.back: A coherent plot lowers uncertainty and improves recall, so it can feel truer than the evidence supports.

reviewCards.front: What is the danger of turning after into because?
reviewCards.back: It treats timing as causality and may hide other causes, missing data, or unresolved links.

reviewCards.front: A story contains real pain. Does that make it decision-ready?
reviewCards.back: No. Respect the pain, then test the causal claims. Real pain can still be attached to an unproven explanation.

reviewCards.front: What words should make you slow down in a narrative?
reviewCards.back: Words like because, therefore, led to, proved, and revealed. Each one should point to evidence.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to keep stories useful by marking causal links and checking which ones are supported before the story drives a decision.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a meeting settles on a neat explanation, then I will write the causal links and ask which links have evidence.
If a presentation says one event caused another, then I will ask what other causes were ruled out.
If a candidate story feels decisive, then I will separate the narrative from measured skills, references, and work samples.
If I keep retelling the same explanation for a problem, then I will name one missing fact that could change the story.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, choose one explanation you have repeated recently. Underline every causal word and mark which links are proven, uncertain, or missing.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, take one strong story from a meeting or article and rewrite it as a list of facts plus open questions.

memorableLines.text: A neat arc is not a proof chain.
